title: Past wind acceleration cut eastern Pacific next-day wind-change error by 3.4% in a 2002-2025 test
abstract: We tested whether the Atlantic forecast gain from past wind acceleration holds in eastern Pacific storms. We used HURDAT2 release 092926 and separate models fit only to earlier seasons from 1982 onward. In 4,684 screened starts from 348 storms in 2002-2025, adding acceleration reduced mean squared error by 3.37%. The conditional 95% three-season block interval was 2.41% to 4.06%. Root mean squared error fell from 15.620 to 15.355 knots. All planned checks gave positive gain intervals. A post hoc check corrected longitude displacement at the date line and gave a 3.23% gain, with limits of 2.51% to 3.74%. This supports a small gain in a second basin under the tested method. It does not establish a physical cause or real-time skill. Revised and rounded winds, future sample selection, one model family and conditional uncertainty limit use. Code, aggregate evidence, exact source hashes, a numerical audit and a figure are included. Raw sources and record-level tables stay external.

display.caption: Eastern Pacific model gains and planned checks in 2002-2025. Intervals use three-season blocks with predictions fixed. The post hoc wrapped-displacement check is reported in the text and aggregate tables.

citations.reason: Replicates its Atlantic added-acceleration test in EP storms, using adapted published code, fixed settings and separate fits.
Related two-basin test of asymmetric persistence; its added term and sample differ.
Wind precision sensitivity motivates measurement limits; no source records or code reused.
